Without it, the browser looks for another page." - wait: 2500 hook: "Long pages such as Wikipedia articles open with a list of contents, and every entry jumps down the page to its part." --- A link can go to another page, or to a place on the same page. On a long page, a menu of links at the top lets people jump straight to the part they want. ## Predict ```step stage: predict code: page.html#jump insight: "Students read href as an address to another page; committing first shows what the # and the matching id do." check: type: predict q: "Someone clicks Results in the menu. What does the page do?" options: - "Scrolls down so the Results heading is at the top" - "Opens a different web page called results" - "Shows only the Results part and hides the rest" - "Nothing: the whole page is already on screen" fault: logic misconception: hash-missing actual: "It scrolls to the Results heading. The link's href names a place on this page, and the heading with that id is the place." ``` The menu links look like links you know, but their `href` values are new. If someone clicks Results, what do you think the page does? ## Run ```step stage: run code: page.html#jump try: { playground: html, starter: "page.html#jump", height: 320 } insight: "A matching name in the id and in the href is all that joins the link to its place." check: { type: reflect, text: "I can say what has to match for a link to jump to a heading." } unlocks: [jump-link] ``` Compare the page with your prediction. Click each link in the menu, then scroll back up. Find the name that appears in both a link and a heading. | Code | What it does | Why | |---|---|---| | `

` | Gives this heading the name `results` | `id` is an attribute, like `href`. The name marks a place on the page, and changes nothing you can see | | `` | Jumps to the element named `results` | The `#` means "on this page". Without it, the browser looks for another page called `results` | | the same name in both places | Joins the link to its place | The names must match exactly, capitals too. If nothing has that id, the link does nothing | | each id used once | Keeps every name pointing at one element | A link can only jump to one place, so two elements with one id means it goes to the first | | the links in a `

Where does the link go?" options: - "To the first one" - "To the second one" - "To both, one after the other" - "Nowhere, because the name is used twice" answer: 0 fault: logic misconception: id-repeats feedback: - null - "The browser looks down the page for the name and stops at the first element it finds." - "A link jumps to one place. It cannot visit two." - "The browser does not check. It takes the first element with that id, so the second can never be reached." explain: "An id names one element. The browser takes the first match, so the second Join part cannot be reached by a link. Give each part its own name." - check: type: bug code: page.html#nohash answer: 4 fault: logic misconception: hash-missing text: "Rules and Join jump down the page, but clicking Results tries to open a different page. Click the line that causes it." explain: "Line 4 has href=\"results\" with no #. Without the #, the browser looks for a page called results instead of an element with that id. It should be href=\"#results\"." ``` ### Where does Join go? Two parts share one name. ```html

Nothing changes on the page yet. ### Link to it Add a menu item that jumps to `meet`. Click it to test. ### Back to the top Name the title `top`, and add a link at the bottom of the page that jumps back to it. ## Mix it up ```step stage: investigate insight: "The menu of links goes in a nav, and the nav is part of the header." check: type: parsons code: page.html#review extra: [""] text: "Put the lines in order to make a header with the title and, inside a nav, a list of two links. One line is not needed." explain: "The header holds the title and the nav. The nav holds the list, and each link sits in its own item. would close a part this page has not opened." ``` A header, a nav and a list of links, all nested inside each other. Put them back together. ## Make ```step stage: make try: { playground: html, starter: "page.html#make", height: 440 } hint: - "Give each heading an id of its own. Then add the `

` with a list of links under the title." - "Each link is ``, with the same name as the id, and the `#` in front." - "Click each link to test it. A link that does nothing has a name that does not match." check: type: code text: "Add a nav in the header with three jump links, and give the three headings the ids rules, results and join." rules: tags: [nav, ul, li, a] contains: - "id=\"rules\"" - "id=\"results\"" - "id=\"join\"" - "href=\"#rules\"" - "href=\"#results\"" - "href=\"#join\"" expected: page.html#sol-make smaller: check: type: question q: "A link says href=\"#rules\". Where does it jump to?" options: - "The element with id=\"rules\"" - "The first heading on the page" - "An element with class=\"rules\"" - "A new page called rules" answer: 0 feedback: - null - "It doesn't jump to the first heading. It jumps to a place with that name." - "A class can be on many elements, so jumps use an id." - "The # means a place on this page, not a different page." explain: "# and a name jump to the element on the page whose id is that name, so the heading needs id=\"rules\"." ``` This page has three parts but no menu. Each link jumps to one of the headings: give them the ids `rules`, `results` and `join`. ```teacher summary: Students name a place on a page with id and link to it with href="#name", so a menu can jump to each part of a long page. time: 40 timing: "Predict and Run 10 min · Investigate 8 min · Modify 8 min · Mix it up 4 min · Make 12 min" goals: - I can give a heading a name with id. - I can link to it with href starting with #. - I can explain why each id is used once and why the # is needed. before: | Do the Make task yourself (about 5 minutes). An **id** is an attribute that gives one element a name. A link whose `href` starts with `#` goes to the element with that name on the same page. The # is the whole difference between "this page" and "another page". Pages need to be long enough to scroll, or the jump is invisible: make the preview small or add a paragraph. running: - "Predict: most students pick the first option, but some think the link opens a new page, because every link they have written so far did. Run it and click each link." - "Run: ask which name appears in both a link and a heading. Then try changing id=\"results\" to id=\"result\": the link stops working and nothing says why. Matching names are all the browser has." - "Modify: name a place, link to it, then link back to the top. After each step, click the new link to test it." - "Investigate: the shared id has no visible symptom except the second part never being reached. Ask them to find it by clicking." - "Make: the check needs the six exact fragments. If it does not tick, compare each href with its id letter by letter." stuck: - see: Clicking a menu link does nothing. ask: Is the name in the href exactly the name in the id, with a # at the front of the href only? fix: Make the two names match letter for letter. Only the href has the #. - see: Clicking a menu link tries to open another page. ask: Does the href start with #? fix: Put a # in front of the name in the href. - see: The id has a # in it, as in id="#join". ask: Where does the # go? fix: The # belongs only in the href. The id is just the name. stretch: "Add a fourth part with its own id and menu link, and a link at the bottom of the page that jumps back to the top (give the heading an id)." support: "Give students the Make starter with the ids already added, and ask them only to build the nav and the links." leads: "Next lesson uses id again: a form label points at its box by id, so clicking the label finds the box. Class idea: find a long page (a Wikipedia article) and look at how its contents list jumps down the page." exit: q: "A menu link has href=\"results\" and a heading has id=\"results\". The link does not jump. What is missing, and why?" a: "The #. href=\"#results\" means the element named results on this page; without it the browser looks for another page called results." explain: | The video and the picture show the same steps: 1. An `id` gives one element a name. Here the heading is named `results`. 2. A link whose `href` starts with `#` jumps to the element with that name. 3. The `#` is the difference. Without it, the browser looks for another page. Each name belongs to one element, so no two elements share an id. solutions: step-4#t1: page.html#sol-id step-4#t2: page.html#sol-link step-4#t3: page.html#sol-top step-6: page.html#sol-make struggle: "Matching the name in the href and the id exactly, and remembering the # in the href only. Have them click every link to test it." class: activities: - at: predict kind: discussion title: Where will it go? minutes: 3 do: | Look at the code. Point to where you think the page will scroll when someone clicks Results, and tell your partner how you know. notes: "Listen for students who point at the link itself. Ask them what in the heading tells the browser this is the place." - at: end kind: activity title: Contents list minutes: 5 do: | Swap pages with a partner. Click every link in their menu. Tell them which link does nothing, and read the name in the link and in the heading aloud. notes: "Most failures are a missing #, a different spelling, or a capital letter.
